headline: Trolled the Wall Till It Died, Anchored Up, Chunked Our Way to Six Yellowfin
subhead: A warm filament pinned to the northeast wall kept the troll bite alive till 10 a.m. — after that, the chunk bag did the work.
body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night to run Wilmington instead of pushing further south to Baltimore, and it came down to fuel math and one look at the imagery. The eddy that's been spinning off the Stream all month is still parked right where I want it, pushing a filament of 78-79°F water up onto the 100-fathom curve on the northeast wall, somewhere around 38°48' N, 74°10' W. That's a 20-mile run I can afford to burn twice if I have to. Baltimore's break looked softer and further offshore — more fuel, less certainty. So Wilmington it was, and I'd make that call again.

We left the dock at 4 a.m. and had lines in by first light, running a standard spread — naked ballyhoo on the long riggers, a green/yellow Ilander-ballyhoo combo down the shotgun, small Joe Shutes on the short corners. The troll bite was real but it wasn't a bonanza — three yellowfin in the 35-50 pound class by 9:30, all right on that temperature seam where the water goes from a milky green to that clean cobalt blue. You could see the color change from the helm, no instruments needed. Once the sun got up high and that seam went slack around 10, the bite died flat. Trolled another ninety minutes for nothing and made the switch.

That's when we ran up-current about a mile, killed the engine over 900 feet of water, and started chunking butterflied bunker off the stern. Took maybe twenty minutes of soaking chunks and a slick before the first fish showed under the boat — and once one showed, they stacked up fast. We put three more yellowfin in the box on the chunk over the next two hours, all on 50-pound fluoro leader, 3/0 circle hooks buried in a bunker chunk, freelined with just enough weight to get it down through the first 30 feet. One bigeye, close to 150 pounds, came up out of nowhere on a bait we'd let sink deeper than the rest — that's the fish that makes the whole day's fuel bill worth it. Six yellowfin and a bigeye for six hours of trolling and three hours at anchor. Not a blowup day, but a solid one, and the kind of numbers that pencil out fine against a 40-mile round trip.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the yellowfin bite would hold steady as long as the high pressure sat over the canyon grounds, and that's exactly how it's played out. The stability up top is keeping that Gulf Stream filament pinned in place instead of sliding off, which means the same stretch of the wall that produced Tuesday should still be productive through the weekend if the weather holds, which right now it looks like it will.

Bluefin are still around but scattered wide — since the July 3rd trophy closure most of what we're seeing are slot fish, 27 to 47 inches, mixed in with the yellowfin on the same temp break. A couple of boats working the canyon this week picked up bluefin on smaller cedar plugs and green machine spreader bars fished tight to the boat, inside 100 feet of wake. Nothing to build a whole trip around, but a welcome bonus if you're already spread out for yellowfin.

Mahi are the wildcard right now — genuinely scattered, not concentrated. We found one decent weedline drifting northeast around 38°42' N, 74°12' W with a scrap of debris holding maybe a dozen fish, 8 to 15 pounds, that jumped all over small skirted ballyhoo and a couple of bubblegum-pink chuggers we threw at them once we spotted the color change. But that's the only real pod we saw all week — most boats are picking off a fish or two incidental to the tuna troll rather than targeting them specifically. If you find floating structure — a pallet, a bucket, anything — it's worth a five-minute stop with a spinning rod and a small bucktail before you move on.

Wahoo showed once, briefly — one fish on a high-speed pass at 38°45' N, 74°08' W, taken on a black-and-purple Ilander with a planer, first thing at dawn before the sun got up. That's a low-percentage play unless you're specifically rigged for it, but worth a mention because it tells you the water column has some real structure to it out there.

White marlin gave us one release Wednesday, a fish that came up on a naked ballyhoo skipping off the left flat line, hooked on a circle and released clean in about four minutes. Scattered reports of one or two more releases elsewhere on the grounds — not a stacked bite, but they're present.

Looking ahead, I'd plan on the same play for the next few days: troll the wall early while that temperature seam is sharp and visible, then be ready to shut down and chunk once the sun kills the surface definition, usually mid-morning. The moon's waxing toward full in early August, which should tighten up current on the grounds and could sharpen the bite further — worth watching for a stronger push of bait onto that eddy edge. If the high pressure breaks down or that filament slides south the way eddies sometimes do, I'd shift attention toward Baltimore before committing another full tank to Wilmington. For now, though, the wall's producing, the fuel math works, and that's the trip I'll keep running until something changes.
